slides.title: Nine hikers cut open their tent and fled in their socks.
Nine never came back
slides.body: In late January 1959 ten experienced hikers led by Igor Dyatlov set out into the northern Urals. One turned back ill. The other nine never returned.

slides.title: Cut from the inside
slides.body: Searchers found the tent on Kholat Syakhl, Mansi for 'Dead Mountain,' cut open from inside. Tracks in socks and bare feet led downhill at -30 °C.

slides.title: Injuries nobody could explain
slides.body: Several bodies had fractured ribs and skulls but little external bruising. Radiation traces on some clothing were later tied to one hiker's job.

slides.title: 'Unknown compelling natural force'
slides.body: That was the Soviet verdict. For 60 years theories ran wild: weapons tests, the KGB, a yeti, aliens. Most can be ruled out for lack of evidence.

slides.title: The 2021 answer
slides.body: Avalanche modeling showed a small slab avalanche fits the evidence: snow bearing down on the tent, the injuries, the timing. Hypothermia did the rest.

caption: A tent cut from the inside, tracks in socks at -30 °C, fractures with little bruising. A 2021 study finally explained it. What was your theory?
